subsection: 1. Employee rights and responsibilities: legislative and non-legislative protection

notes.h: Rights and responsibilities: who protects an employee
notes.b: An employee works under the direction of an employer, in return for wages or a salary, which is what separates an employee from a self-employed person. The law and a range of agreements protect that relationship, and every right has a matching responsibility.
points: An employer hires an employee under a contract of employment, and the employee works under the employer's direction and is paid wages or salary, unlike a self-employed person who runs their own business.

Legislative protection comes from the law, so it applies to all workers and no contract can reduce it. Non-legislative protection comes from agreements and procedures, such as contracts, collective agreements, handbooks and codes of practice.

Employees have rights, such as fair pay and a safe workplace, and responsibilities, such as following lawful instructions. Employers have matching responsibilities: pay, a safe workplace, non-discrimination and fair procedures.

Ethically, the law sets the floor and good employers go further, building inclusive workplaces with dignity at work and care for staff wellbeing (corporate wellness). Safe, decent and secure work is also the social side of a sustainable business (the S in ESG).
notes.tip: Common mistakes are giving only the employee's rights and forgetting responsibilities, and treating a handbook policy as if it were law. Give both sides, and keep law and non-legislative protection apart.

notes.h: Pay and the national minimum wage
notes.b: Pay protection in Irish law combines a legal floor on hourly rates with rules on how and when wages are paid. Gross pay is what the employer owes, deductions are what is taken off, and the law controls both.
points: The National Minimum Wage Act 2000 sets a legal minimum hourly rate, and an employer cannot pay a worker less than the rate that applies. Reduced rates apply to workers under 20.

The government reviews the minimum rate, usually after recommendations from the Low Pay Commission (the independent body that advises it each year). Each change affects employers' costs and workers' take-home pay.
For example, the adult rate rose from 13.50 euro to 14.15 euro an hour on 1 January 2026, and a rise to 14.94 euro from 1 January 2027 was announced in Budget 2027 (October 2026).
The Payment of Wages Act 1991 requires employers to pay wages on time and to give employees a written statement of pay and deductions, so a worker can check that the pay is right.
Deductions from wages are allowed only where the law permits them or where the employee has agreed to them in writing, which stops an employer taking money off pay at will.
A worker who is not paid properly, such as a sample worker paid below the minimum wage, can make a complaint to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).
notes.tip: Naming an Act without saying what it does is a common mistake. Pair the Act with its right, and say where the worker complains. Do not quote rates without the date.

notes.b: Conditions of employment cover how much a person works, what they are told about the job and what leave they can take. Several Acts set the minimum standards, and an employer cannot go below them.
points: The Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 limits average weekly working hours and guarantees rest breaks, daily and weekly rest periods, and annual leave, so workers are not overworked without rest.
The Terms of Employment (Information) Acts require employers to give employees a written statement of core terms, such as pay, hours and place of work, so both sides know what was agreed.

The Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 restricts zero-hours contracts (contracts with no guaranteed hours), with exceptions for genuine emergencies and short-term relief for routine absences.

It also guarantees a minimum payment when an employee is called in but not given the expected work, and gives banded hours, based on the hours worked in the previous 12 months, to those whose contract does not reflect the hours they actually work.
The Sick Leave Act 2022 gives eligible employees a statutory right to paid sick leave, with the number of paid days set in law. As of 2025 the WRC states the entitlement is 5 days a year.

The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 gives employees a right to request remote working, and parents and carers a right to request flexible working. It also provides five days' unpaid medical care leave in 12 months for family and carers.
Digital working makes remote requests practical, and employers often keep employees' time and pay records electronically.
notes.tip: Say the 2018 Act restricts zero-hours contracts, with exceptions, rather than bans them. Do not quote hour limits, leave days or break lengths unless you are sure of them.

notes.b: Work can injure people, so the law makes safety a duty on both employer and employee. The main law is the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005, enforced by the Health and Safety Authority (HSA).
points: The HSA can prosecute breaches of the Act, so safety duties are enforceable obligations and not just good practice.

Employers must identify hazards (things that could cause harm), assess the risks, prepare a safety statement (a written plan for managing safety), and provide training, information and safe equipment.

Employees must take reasonable care of their own safety and that of others, use the protective equipment provided, and report hazards and accidents, because the employer can only fix what it knows about.
An employee who reasonably believes there is a serious and imminent risk can refuse to work on it, and cannot be penalised for doing so.
notes.tip: Give both the employer's duties and the employee's duties, and name the HSA as the enforcer.

notes.b: The Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015 protect employees and job applicants from unfair treatment at work. They apply to full-time, part-time and temporary staff in the public and private sectors.
points: The Acts cover recruitment, pay, training, promotion, conditions of employment and dismissal. They also prohibit sexual harassment and victimisation.
The nine protected grounds are gender, civil status, family status, sexual orientation, religion, age, disability, race, and membership of the Traveller community.
Race includes colour, nationality and ethnic or national origins, so colour is part of race and not a separate tenth ground.

Direct discrimination means a person is treated less favourably because of a protected ground. Indirect discrimination means a rule that applies to everyone but disadvantages people on a ground, unless it is objectively justified.
An employer must provide reasonable accommodation for a disabled employee, such as adapted equipment, unless doing so would be a disproportionate burden.
Discrimination claims are made to the Workplace Relations Commission.
Ethically, equal treatment and dignity at work make an inclusive workplace, and employers can go beyond what the Acts require.
notes.tip: If asked for three grounds other than gender, give three of the nine exactly, such as age, disability and race. Common mistakes are repeating gender, writing colour as a separate ground, and inventing grounds such as political opinion or weight.

notes.b: Employees need to know they cannot lose a job without good reason. The Unfair Dismissals Acts 1977 to 2015 protect employees who have the required length of service.
points: Generally 12 months' continuous service is needed to claim, but not for dismissal for trade union membership or a protected disclosure.
A dismissal is fair only if it is for a fair reason, such as capability, conduct, redundancy, a legal prohibition or another substantial reason, and the employer follows fair procedures.
Redundancy is a fair ground when the proper procedures are followed, so it is not the same as unfair dismissal.
Some reasons, such as trade union membership or raising a safety complaint, make a dismissal automatically unfair, because the law protects workers who use their rights.
Constructive dismissal occurs when an employee resigns because the employer's conduct makes continued employment unreasonable, and the law treats the resignation as a dismissal.
Redress for unfair dismissal may be reinstatement (getting the old job back), re-engagement (a new or different job with the employer) or compensation, decided by the WRC or the Labour Court.
notes.tip: Keep unfair dismissal and redundancy apart. Do not quote notice periods or compensation caps.

notes.b: A right is only useful if a worker can enforce it. Two bodies hear employment complaints, and the order matters.
points: The WRC (set up under the Workplace Relations Act 2015) investigates and adjudicates on most employment complaints, including pay, discrimination, dismissal and working time claims. It is the first hearing.
The Labour Court hears appeals from WRC decisions and handles certain industrial relations disputes.

Employees usually must make a complaint within a set time limit, so acting promptly protects the claim. For unfair dismissal it is normally 6 months from dismissal, extendable by up to a further 6 months for reasonable cause.
notes.tip: A common mistake is mixing up the WRC and the Labour Court: the WRC is the first hearing and the Labour Court is the appeal.

notes.b: Rights come with duties. The employer's side of the bargain is pay, a safe workplace, non-discrimination and fair procedures, and the employee's side is below.
points: Employees must follow reasonable and lawful instructions from their employer and attend work as rostered, because the business depends on staff being where they are needed.
Employees owe a duty of good faith, which includes not disclosing confidential business information and not competing unfairly with the employer.
When resigning, employees must give the notice required by their contract or by law.
notes.tip: A full answer on rights also covers responsibilities, for both employee and employer.

notes.b: Protection also comes from agreements and procedures that sit alongside the law. These are not Acts, so each depends on what was agreed, but none can reduce statutory rights.
points: An employment contract sets out the express terms agreed by employer and employee, and sits alongside statutory rights, which cannot be signed away.
A collective agreement is negotiated between a trade union and an employer, and sets pay and conditions for a group of workers.
HR policies in a staff handbook, such as a sample business's rules on conduct, set expected conduct and procedures, and they cannot reduce statutory rights.
Codes of practice, such as the Code of Practice on Grievance and Disciplinary Procedures (S.I. 146 of 2000), give practical guidance that bodies such as the WRC take into account.
The code was drafted by the former Labour Relations Commission and is now maintained by the WRC. A code is guidance, not an Act.
A grievance procedure lets an employee raise a complaint informally and then formally, through a set sequence of steps.
notes.tip: Treating a handbook policy as law is a common mistake. In a discuss question, weigh legislative protection (law, applies to all workers, cannot be signed away) against non-legislative protection, give three or four developed points and reach a conclusion.

notes.b: Examining both kinds of protection means seeing what each does best. Law sets a floor for everyone, while agreements and procedures can fit a particular workplace.
points: Legislation applies to all workers and is enforced by bodies such as the WRC and HSA, so it gives the strongest and most uniform protection, but it sets only minimum standards.
Contracts, collective agreements and handbooks can give more than the law, such as better pay for a group, but they bind only the parties to them and cannot go below the law.
For the business, meeting legal standards costs money, but fairer, safer and more secure staff are often more productive, so good employers may go beyond the minimum.
notes.tip: A discuss answer can weigh the cost to the business of meeting standards against fairer, safer and more productive staff. Name the Act with its year, state the right, say who enforces it, and link it to the effect on employee and business.

keyTerms.definition: A legal minimum hourly rate that employers must pay workers, set under the National Minimum Wage Act 2000.
A resignation forced by the employer's conduct, which the law treats as a dismissal.
Less favourable treatment of a person because of a protected ground, such as age or race.
A rule or practice that applies to everyone but disadvantages people on a protected ground, without objective justification.
Changes an employer makes so that a disabled employee can do the job, unless this would be a disproportionate burden.
A written document setting out an employer's safety and health arrangements, based on the risks identified at work.
A State body that investigates and decides many employment complaints and disputes.
An agreement on pay and conditions negotiated between a union and an employer, covering a group of workers.
A set sequence of steps by which an employee raises a complaint about their employment.

factCards.term: Nine grounds of discrimination under the Employment Equality Acts
factCards.definition: Gender, civil status, family status, sexual orientation, religion, age, disability, race, and membership of the Traveller community.

factCards.term: Employer duties under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act
factCards.definition: Identify hazards, assess risks, prepare a safety statement, and provide training, information and safe equipment.

factCards.term: Employee duties under the same Act
factCards.definition: Take reasonable care of their own and others' safety, use protective equipment, and report hazards and accidents.
Capability, conduct, redundancy, a legal prohibition, or another substantial reason, applied with fair procedures.
The WRC investigates and adjudicates; the Labour Court hears appeals.
Legislation sets rights for all workers; contracts, collective agreements, handbooks and codes of practice add further protection.

questions.prompt: Discuss how legislation protects employees in relation to pay, working conditions and health and safety, and explain the role of the WRC in enforcing these rights.
questions.model: On pay, the National Minimum Wage Act 2000 sets a legal floor for hourly rates, and the Payment of Wages Act 1991 requires wages to be paid on time with a written statement of pay and deductions. On conditions, the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 limits average working hours and guarantees rest breaks and annual leave, while the Sick Leave Act 2022 gives a right to paid sick leave. On health and safety, the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 requires employers to assess risks and provide training and safe equipment, and it requires employees to take reasonable care. The WRC enforces many of these rights by investigating complaints and deciding claims on pay, working time, discrimination and dismissal, with appeals going to the Labour Court.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between direct and indirect discrimination, and give an example of each in an Irish workplace.
questions.model: Direct discrimination occurs when a person is treated less favourably because of a protected ground, such as refusing to promote an employee because of their age. Indirect discrimination occurs when a rule that applies to everyone disadvantages people on a protected ground, such as requiring full-time evening shifts that make it very hard for a carer to take a job, unless the employer can show the rule is objectively justified.

questions.prompt: Outline two reasons why a dismissal may be fair, and explain what constructive dismissal means.
questions.model: A dismissal may be fair for capability, where an employee cannot do the job to the required standard, or for conduct, where an employee has breached discipline. Constructive dismissal occurs when an employee resigns because the employer's conduct makes continued employment unreasonable, and the law treats that resignation as a dismissal.
